tldr: A 3-stage progressive imitation framework that learns terrain-appropriate humanoid parkour skills and subsequently relaxes imitation constraints to adapt hand-knee contact placement to the robot's own body. Evaluated on a real humanoid robot, it completed continuous parkour runs over obstacles up to 1 m high without real-world policy fine-tuning.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed learning framework. On the right, human motion data is retargeted into physically executable robot references. In the center, a multi-head discriminator (AMP) guides terrain-indexed skill acquisition. At the bottom, the geometric support guidance module flexibly adapts hand and knee contact placements to the robot's physical morphology.
overview:
When teaching a humanoid robot extreme parkour skills like wall climbing or vaulting, imitating human motion capture demonstrations is a promising approach. However, humans and robots differ significantly in limb proportions, actuator torque limits, and accessible support surfaces. Consequently, forcing a robot to rigidly trace human contact patterns leads to physical breakdowns or causes the robot to fall when the terrain shifts even slightly.

To tackle this, the authors designed a progressive approach: use imitation as scaffolding to acquire skills, and then relax the motion prior constraints as training proceeds, allowing the robot's own geometric support adaptation to take over. Specifically, the framework first generates physically feasible robot reference rollouts, then acquires terrain-appropriate skills via terrain-indexed adversarial motion priors (AMP). In the final stage, the motion-prior weight is halved while candidate-based precontact attraction and actual-contact evaluation—derived from obstacle edges and surface geometry—are introduced, encouraging the robot to explore stable support postures without prescribing a fixed contact sequence.

The framework was evaluated on a 23-DoF real humanoid robot, the Noetix E1, across 0.4 m (Low), 0.6 m (Mid), and 1.0 m (High) obstacles, as well as concatenated hybrid obstacle courses. In simulation, the policy achieved a 96.34% hybrid course traversal success rate, significantly outperforming single-AMP and skill distillation baselines.

Remarkably, when transferred zero-shot to the physical robot without real-world policy fine-tuning, the policy completed 29 out of 30 individual obstacle trials and 4 out of 5 hybrid course runs. These results demonstrate the power of learning general movement intentions from human demonstrations while releasing contact details to match the robot's own morphology and the environment's geometry.
contributions: A 3-stage progressive imitation framework that acquires skills from human demonstrations and subsequently relaxes their constraints to adapt to robot-specific contact configurations.
Terrain-indexed adversarial motion priors (AMP) featuring a shared feature backbone and per-terrain discriminator heads to prevent interference between walking and parkour maneuvers.
Geometric support guidance that pairs precontact attraction with actual-contact retention rewards without prescribing a contact sequence.
Demonstration of continuous parkour runs and out-of-distribution obstacle robustness on a physical humanoid (Noetix E1) using a single deployed policy without external skill labels.

sections.heading: Why Direct Imitation of Human Parkour Fails
sections.summary: Direct imitation breaks down in full-body humanoid parkour due to morphological and actuator disparities between humans and robots. This paper introduces a 3-stage progressive approach: use imitation to build a skill foundation, then gradually relax its influence to adapt hand-knee geometric support.
sections.details:
Full-body parkour—where a humanoid overcomes obstacles using its entire body—unlocks agile locomotion far beyond conventional bipedal walking. Leaping onto, supporting on, vaulting over, and landing from obstacles requires tightly coordinated full-body contacts across the hands, knees, and feet. While human demonstrations offer rich behavioral references, differences in body proportions, torque limitations, and reachable support geometries mean that directly reproducing human motion leads to fundamental limitations.

Three intertwined challenges arise:
- Direct retargeting of human motion violates physical limits such as joint limits and actuator torque capacities.
- Even with physically executable references, determining which skill fits a given terrain is non-trivial.
- Forcing the robot to follow human contact sequences prevents it from exploring alternative, feasible contact placements (such as where to place hands or knees) suited to its own morphology.

In short, physical executability, terrain appropriateness, and robot-specific support adaptation are distinct challenges. The core design principle of this work is to treat imitation learning as scaffolding for skill acquisition. Once foundational skills are learned, the influence of motion priors is relaxed and geometric support guidance is amplified. This preserves the overarching traversal intent while allowing the physical contact execution to adapt flexibly to the robot's physical constraints.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Parkour Control, Motion Priors, and Contact Guidance
sections.summary: Prior work spans RL-based visual parkour, multi-skill extensions of adversarial motion priors (AMP), and foothold guidance. This work unifies these directions, introducing geometric support for full-body contact (hands and knees) alongside dynamic relaxation of the motion prior.
sections.details:
To place this work in context, it builds upon three main research threads.

### II-A Vision-Based Full-Body Parkour
While quadrupeds have achieved blind and vision-based obstacle traversal without reference motions, humanoids present higher degrees of freedom and greater instability, making human motion data a standard reference. Prior methods, such as APEX or Perceptive Humanoid Parkour, train individual expert policies for each skill and distill them into a single policy. Instead of distillation, this work directly handles skill acquisition and contact adaptation within a single policy by pairing motion priors with geometric support guidance.

### II-B Multi-Skill and Conditional Motion Priors (AMP)
Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP) offer a powerful framework that blends task rewards with discriminator-driven style rewards to encourage natural motions. However, packing diverse skills into a single discriminator causes common walking behaviors to conflict with infrequent jumping or vaulting motions. Prior methods explored conditional or multi-discriminator architectures. This paper extends AMP inputs beyond kinematics to include torques, contact states, and yaw-aligned local height scans, directly evaluating the dynamic consistency between terrain and movement.

### II-C Contact Priors in Robot Locomotion
Prior works have leveraged geometric guidance for foot placements (such as CReF or SSR guiding feet to stable landing candidates). However, these largely focus on feet. In extreme parkour, where the robot places its hands and knees becomes a matter of survival. This work sets itself apart by generating geometric candidates that account for the distinct reachability and support roles of hands versus knees, guiding limbs both before and during contact.

sections.heading: A 3-Stage Training Pipeline and Geometric Support Guidance
sections.summary: The proposed method consists of reference trajectory refinement (Stage 1), terrain-indexed AMP skill learning (Stage 2), and contact adaptation via relaxed AMP and hand-knee geometric support (Stage 3). At deployment, the policy runs autonomously using only onboard depth and proprioception, requiring no external skill labels.
sections.details:
The complete pipeline evolves the role of imitation across three progressive stages.

### III-A Framework Overview and 3-Stage Training
- **Stage 1 (Privileged Imitation)**: Human motion data is retargeted to the robot's kinematic structure, and privileged imitation in simulation (incorporating torque limits and contacts) produces physically executable reference rollouts.
- **Stage 2 (Skill Acquisition)**: Using reference pools organized by terrain category, terrain-indexed AMP guides the policy to acquire terrain-appropriate traversal skills.
- **Stage 3 (Support Adaptation)**: The AMP weight $\beta$ is halved from $1.0$ to $0.5$, while the geometric support reward weight $\alpha$ for hands and knees is ramped from $0$ to $1$. This shifts the policy away from rigidly copying human contact sequences toward robot-specific contact placements.

The policy operates in an asymmetric actor-critic setup. The actor takes a 129-dimensional input: a 78-dimensional proprioceptive and velocity command history (compressed via a HIM module into estimated velocities and a 16-dimensional latent vector) combined with 32-dimensional features from a $24\times 24$ onboard depth image. It then predicts target joint positions through four gated expert layers. Privileged information like ground-truth height scans and terrain labels are used only during training; deployment relies entirely on onboard sensors.

### III-B Terrain-Indexed Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP)
The discriminator utilizes a shared height-scan encoder, a shared feature trunk (hidden layers 512, 256), and four independent output heads corresponding to terrain classes (Low, Mid, High, Flat). The input is an expanded 402-dimensional vector containing joint positions and velocities, 24 local body keypoint positions, root velocity, contact flags, joint torques, and yaw-aligned height scans. Basic standing and walking motions are included across all terrain pools to prevent degradation of daily locomotion while learning terrain-specific parkour maneuvers.

### III-C Geometric Support Guidance for Hands and Knees
Rather than enforcing a hardcoded contact sequence, stable support is encouraged via a two-stage geometric reward formulation:
- **Precontact Attraction**: Support candidate points satisfying surface normals, flatness, and clearance are sampled from obstacle tops and edges. Reachable candidates (up to 8) are selected using limb-specific ellipsoidal volumes around anchor joints. The reward increases as the limb's predicted position $\hat{p}_\ell = p_\ell + \delta \dot{p}_\ell$ (with $\delta=0.12$ s) approaches candidate points.
- **Actual Contact Evaluation**: When contact occurs, the policy is rewarded if contact points maintain sufficient clearance from surface mask edges and bear adequate normal force. Furthermore, on high obstacles ($\ge 0.9$ m), a multi-point lateral hold posture (at least two valid contacts including hands) is latched and evaluated. This combination of attraction and evaluation naturally yields safe, non-slipping contact placements without dictating an exact sequence.

Stage 3 relaxes the motion prior while introducing precontact attraction and actual-contact evaluation from geometric support candidates.

sections.heading: Impressive Success Rates: Dominant Performance in Simulation and Real World
sections.summary: In simulation, the proposed method achieved a 96.34% success rate on continuous hybrid courses, outperforming all baselines. In zero-shot physical deployment on the Noetix E1, it completed 29 of 30 individual trials and 4 of 5 continuous hybrid courses, confirming the power of contact adaptation.
sections.details:
To evaluate the framework, extensive experiments were conducted in simulation (Isaac Lab) and on a physical humanoid (Noetix E1: 23 DoF, powered by a Jetson Orin NX).

### IV-A Benchmark Comparison (Simulation)
Policies were evaluated across three individual obstacle heights (Low: 0.4 m, Mid: 0.6 m, High: 1.0 m), a concatenated hybrid course of all three, and out-of-distribution (OOD) heights varying by 1–3 cm (2,048 environments per condition).
- **Proposed Method (Ours)**: Achieved stellar traversal rates: 100% on Low, 98.44% on Mid, 98.14% on High, 96.34% on the hybrid course, and 93.46% under OOD conditions.
- **Baselines**: Velocity Tracking without AMP and Single AMP collapsed to near-0% success on High obstacles and the hybrid course. Multi-Skill Distillation performed well on Low and Mid, but dropped to 64.75% on High and 73.83% on the hybrid course, clearly highlighting the superiority of the proposed framework.
- **Ablations**: Removing Stage 2 (AMP skill acquisition) dropped hybrid success to 0%. Omitting Stage 3 (support adaptation) reduced High success to 79.69% and hybrid success to 83.59%.

### IV-B Terrain-Skill Temporal Alignment
Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) analysis was used to inspect whether the policy autonomously switches skills during continuous runs. Comparing joint angle trajectories against reference motions showed that as the robot approached the High obstacle, DTW distance to the High reference was minimal (1.50–4.88 s), subsequently shifting to Mid (4.88–8.00 s) and Low (8.00–12.54 s). Motion transitions occurred smoothly relying solely on vision and proprioception, without external skill switches.

### IV-C Ablation of Support Adaptation
To evaluate the impact of Stage 3 contact adaptation, a challenging lateral traversal task on a narrow $1\times 1$ m platform (1 m high) was tested. Removing support candidate rewards (w/o Candidates) dropped the success rate to 46.24%, while keeping the motion prior unrelaxed (w/o Relaxation) fell to 58.89%, compared to 93.46% for the proposed method. When imitation constraints remained rigid, the robot placed hands dangerously close to platform edges and slipped. In contrast, the adapted policy placed hands securely inward.

### IV-D Real-World Zero-Shot Deployment
The single policy trained in simulation was directly transferred to the Noetix E1 without fine-tuning. It completed 10/10 trials on Low, 9/10 on Mid, and 10/10 on High (29/30 total single-obstacle trials). Furthermore, it completed 4 out of 5 runs on the continuous hybrid course and succeeded in 13/15 trials on out-of-distribution heights. The learned geometric support adaptation proved remarkably robust against real-world sim-to-real dynamics discrepancies.

As the robot traverses obstacles, the reference with the lowest distance smoothly transitions from High to Mid to Low, demonstrating autonomous vision-based skill selection under a single policy.

In the bottom row (proposed method), geometric guidance leads the robot to securely place its hands further inward in both simulation and the real world.

sections.heading: From Imitation to Adaptation: A New Blueprint for Extreme Humanoid Locomotion
sections.summary: This study presented a framework that learns skills via terrain-indexed motion priors and then relaxes the prior to enable geometric support adaptation. Dominant parkour performance in simulation and on real hardware confirms the value of separating and reconciling human imitation with robot-specific contact adaptation.
sections.details:
This paper demonstrated a progressive imitation learning framework that acquires parkour skills from human demonstrations and subsequently evolves contact behaviors to match the robot's physical support needs.

The philosophy of using imitation as an initial stepping stone and then relaxing its constraints to unlock geometric support adaptation provides a highly generalizable pathway to bridge human-robot morphological discrepancies. The fact that the physical Noetix E1 humanoid conquered 1 m obstacles and continuous courses with zero real-world policy fine-tuning marks a notable milestone in full-body humanoid locomotion control.

For future work, the authors highlight expanding reference motion diversity and developing real-time candidate generation algorithms capable of handling irregular, non-flat, and unstructured rubble.

takeaways: Treating imitation as initial scaffolding and relaxing it later is key to bridging human-robot morphological gaps.
Using terrain-indexed multi-head AMP with torque, contact, and local height scans prevents standard walking and extreme parkour skills from interfering with each other.
Guiding limbs via precontact attraction and actual-contact evaluation fosters flexible, emergent hand and knee placements without hardcoding contact sequences.
A single policy driven solely by onboard depth, proprioception, and velocity commands can achieve zero-shot continuous parkour on physical humanoids when paired with a history estimator (HIM).
limitations: Support candidate generation currently assumes planar surfaces; handling non-staircase rubble and irregular curved geometries remains an open challenge.
Real-world failures occasionally involved insufficient arm support or skill misinterpretations, such as selecting overly acrobatic behaviors for low obstacles.
Training iterations for Stage 2 and Stage 3 were kept fixed, leaving the isolated contributions of extra training steps versus individual loss components incompletely disentangled.
